questions.explain: An abelian variety is a connected projective group variety; commutativity is a *consequence* via the rigidity lemma, not part of the definition. Affine algebraic groups (e.g. $\mathbb{G}_m$) and non-projective complex tori are excluded.
questions.q: Which of the following is the cleanest correct definition of an abelian variety over a field $k$?
choices: A connected projective group variety over $k$.
Any commutative group scheme of finite type over $k$.
A complex torus $V/\Lambda$ with $\dim V \ge 1$.
A smooth proper variety with trivial canonical bundle.

questions.explain: Over $\mathbb{C}$, $A(\mathbb{C}) \cong V/\Lambda$ with $V \cong \mathbb{C}^g$ and $\Lambda \cong \mathbb{Z}^{2g}$, so the underlying real torus has dimension $2g = 6$ for $g=3$.
questions.q: Let $A$ be an abelian variety of dimension $g$ over $\mathbb{C}$. As a real Lie group, $A(\mathbb{C})$ is homeomorphic to a torus $(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^d$. What is $d$ when $g = 3$?

questions.explain: Rigidity forces commutativity and the morphism-as-translation-plus-homomorphism statement. $H^1(A,\mathcal{O}_A)$ is the tangent space of the dual abelian variety $A^\vee$, hence has dimension $\dim A$. Abelian varieties are *not* rational — every nontrivial $1$-form $\omega \in H^0(A,\Omega^1)$ is nowhere vanishing and translation-invariant, obstructing rationality.
questions.q: Which statements are true for any abelian variety $A$ over an algebraically closed field $k$? Select all that apply.
choices: The group law on $A(k)$ is automatically commutative.
$A$ is rational (i.e. birational to projective space) for $\dim A \ge 1$.
Every regular map $A \to B$ between abelian varieties is the composition of a translation and a homomorphism.
The structure sheaf cohomology $H^0(A, \mathcal{O}_A) = k$ and $H^1(A, \mathcal{O}_A)$ has dimension $\dim A$.

questions.explain: $A^\vee = \mathrm{Pic}^0(A)$, the connected component of the Picard scheme: it classifies line bundles whose first Chern class is zero, i.e. those that are translation-invariant up to isomorphism.
questions.q: What does the dual abelian variety $A^\vee$ parameterize?
choices: Degree-zero line bundles on $A$, modulo isomorphism.
All line bundles on $A$, modulo translation.
Subvarieties of $A$ of codimension one.
Effective divisors on $A$.

questions.explain: A complex torus is projective (hence algebraic) iff it admits a Riemann form — a positive-definite Hermitian $H$ on $V$ with $\operatorname{Im} H(\Lambda,\Lambda) \subset \mathbb{Z}$. For $g=1$ this is automatic; for $g \ge 2$ a generic torus has none, so most complex tori are not algebraic.
questions.q: Over $\mathbb{C}$, when does a complex torus $V/\Lambda$ admit the structure of an abelian variety?
choices: Always — every complex torus is algebraic.
Iff $\dim V \le 2$.
Iff there exists a positive-definite Hermitian form $H$ on $V$ whose imaginary part is integer-valued on $\Lambda$ (a polarization).
Iff the lattice $\Lambda$ is generated by orthogonal vectors.

questions.explain: Principal means the polarization is an isomorphism, equivalently all $d_i = 1$. Then $\deg \lambda = 1^2 = 1$.
questions.q: A polarization $\lambda\colon A \to A^\vee$ has type $(d_1, d_2, \dots, d_g)$ with $d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \cdots \mid d_g$, and $\deg \lambda = (d_1 d_2 \cdots d_g)^2$. For a principal polarization on a $4$-dimensional abelian variety, what is $\deg \lambda$?

questions.explain: $[n]\colon A\to A$ has degree $n^{2g}$, and is étale when $n$ is invertible in $k$. So $A[n](\bar k) \cong (\mathbb{Z}/n)^{2g}$ as an abelian group. For $g=2,n=5$: $5^{2\cdot 2}=625$.
questions.q: Let $A$ be an abelian variety of dimension $g = 2$ over $\bar k$ with $\mathrm{char}\,k \ne 5$. What is $\#A[5](\bar k)$?

questions.explain: The Weil conjectures (proved for abelian varieties by Weil himself) say each Frobenius eigenvalue is an algebraic integer with $|\alpha_i| = q^{1/2}$ in every complex embedding. The characteristic polynomial $P(T) = \prod(T-\alpha_i)$ has integer coefficients and degree $2g$.
questions.q: For an abelian variety $A/\mathbb{F}_q$ of dimension $g$, the Frobenius endomorphism acts on $T_\ell A \otimes \mathbb{Q}_\ell$ with eigenvalues $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{2g}$. What is $|\alpha_i|$ as a complex number under any embedding $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$?
choices: $\sqrt q$
It depends on $A$ and is not fixed.

questions.explain: All four are correct: the rank is $2g$, the Galois action is continuous, the principal polarization yields a Weil pairing landing in the cyclotomic Tate twist, and Tate's theorem (1966) for finite fields — generalised by Faltings (1983) for number fields — recovers $\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_\ell$ from the Galois module $\mathrm{Hom}(T_\ell A, T_\ell B)$.
questions.q: Which of the following are true about the Tate module $T_\ell A$ of an abelian variety $A$ of dimension $g$ over a field $k$ with $\ell$ invertible in $k$? Select all that apply.
choices: $T_\ell A$ is a free $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$-module of rank $2g$.
$\mathrm{Gal}(\bar k/k)$ acts $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$-linearly and continuously on $T_\ell A$.
The Weil pairing gives a Galois-equivariant alternating pairing $T_\ell A \times T_\ell A \to \mathbb{Z}_\ell(1)$.
The functor $A \mapsto T_\ell A$ is fully faithful on isogeny classes (Tate's isogeny conjecture for finite-base-field $k$).

questions.explain: $\mathrm{Jac}(C) = \mathrm{Pic}^0(C)$ has dimension $g$ — equal to $\dim H^0(C, \Omega^1_C)$, the genus.
questions.q: Let $C$ be a smooth projective curve of genus $g = 5$ over $\mathbb{C}$. What is the dimension of its Jacobian $\mathrm{Jac}(C)$ as an abelian variety?

questions.explain: Torelli says the polarized Jacobian determines the curve. The unpolarized Jacobian does *not* — distinct curves can have isomorphic underlying abelian varieties. The Schottky problem asks which p.p.a.v.'s actually arise from curves; for $g \ge 4$ the Jacobian locus is a proper closed subvariety of $\mathcal{A}_g$.
questions.q: Which statement most accurately captures the Torelli theorem?
choices: Two curves of the same genus always have isomorphic Jacobians.
The Jacobian of a curve $C$ of genus $g \ge 1$, equipped with its principal polarization, determines $C$ up to isomorphism.
Every principally polarized abelian variety arises as a Jacobian.
Jacobians of curves are the only simple abelian varieties.

questions.explain: The theta divisor is the image of $\mathrm{Sym}^{g-1}(C)$ — a divisor (codim 1) inside the $g$-dimensional Jacobian, classifying degree-$(g-1)$ effective divisors. The map from $\mathrm{Sym}^g(C)$ is surjective (Abel–Jacobi) so it lands on a divisor only when $g=1$. The class of $\Theta$ provides the canonical principal polarization.
questions.q: On $\mathrm{Jac}(C)$ for $C$ of genus $g$, the theta divisor $\Theta$ is built as the image of which Abel–Jacobi map?
choices: $C \to \mathrm{Jac}(C)$, $p \mapsto [p - p_0]$.
$\mathrm{Sym}^{g-1}(C) \to \mathrm{Jac}(C)$, $(p_1,\dots,p_{g-1}) \mapsto [p_1 + \cdots + p_{g-1} - (g-1)p_0]$.
$\mathrm{Sym}^{g}(C) \to \mathrm{Jac}(C)$, $(p_1,\dots,p_g) \mapsto [p_1 + \cdots + p_g - g p_0]$.
$C \times C \to \mathrm{Jac}(C)$, $(p,q) \mapsto [p - q]$.

questions.explain: The Néron mapping property is the universal extension of $K$-points from smooth tests. It singles out the Néron model uniquely; in particular it forces $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{O}_K) = A(K)$. Néron models are usually *not* projective — properness fails outside the good-reduction case.
questions.q: What is the defining (Néron mapping) property of the Néron model $\mathcal{A}$ of an abelian variety $A/K$ over the DVR $\mathcal{O}_K$?
choices: $\mathcal{A}$ is the unique projective smooth model of $A$ over $\mathcal{O}_K$.

$\mathcal{A}$ is the smooth separated $\mathcal{O}_K$-scheme of finite type with $\mathcal{A}_K = A$ such that for every smooth $\mathcal{O}_K$-scheme $T$, every $K$-map $T_K \to A$ extends uniquely to $T \to \mathcal{A}$.
$\mathcal{A}$ is the regular minimal model.
$\mathcal{A}$ is any smooth $\mathcal{O}_K$-group scheme whose generic fibre is $A$.

questions.explain: Good reduction means $\mathcal{A}_k$ is *proper* (equivalently, an abelian variety). Semistable reduction relaxes this to: $\mathcal{A}_k^0$ is an extension of an abelian variety by a torus (no unipotent part). Additive reduction is the rest. The conductor equals $1$ at unramified places of good reduction.
questions.q: An abelian variety $A/K$ has *good reduction* at the closed point of $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{O}_K$ iff:
choices: the special fibre $\mathcal{A}_k$ of the Néron model is again an abelian variety;
$A(K)$ is finite;
all Tate-module elements have finite order;
the conductor of $A$ equals $1$.

questions.explain: For type $I_n$ ($n \ge 1$, multiplicative reduction) the component group is cyclic of order $n$ — the special fibre is a Néron $n$-gon, so $\Phi \cong \mathbb{Z}/n$. For $n=4$, $|\Phi|=4$. (For additive types $II, III, IV, II^*, III^*, IV^*$ one reads $|\Phi|$ off Kodaira's table; types $I_n^*$ give $|\Phi| \in \{2,4\}$.)
questions.q: An elliptic curve $E/K$ over a local field has Kodaira reduction type $I_4$ (multiplicative, $v(\Delta) = 4$). What is the order of the component group $\Phi = \mathcal{E}_k/\mathcal{E}_k^0$?

questions.explain: Mordell–Weil: for any number field $K$ and abelian variety $A/K$, $A(K) \cong \mathbb{Z}^r \oplus A(K)_{\mathrm{tors}}$ with $r$ finite (the rank) and torsion finite. The proof goes through weak Mordell–Weil ($A(K)/nA(K)$ finite via Galois cohomology) plus an infinite descent argument using heights.
questions.q: Which finiteness statement is the Mordell–Weil theorem for abelian varieties?
choices: $A(\bar K)$ is finite.
$A(K)$ is finite.
$A(K)$ is finitely generated as an abelian group.
The torsion subgroup $A(K)_{\mathrm{tors}}$ is bounded uniformly in $A$.

questions.explain: The Shafarevich-style statement Faltings proved: principally polarized abelian varieties over $K$ of fixed dimension $g$ with good reduction outside a fixed finite set $S$ form finitely many isomorphism classes. Combined with Kodaira's parameter argument applied to Jacobians, this implies Mordell's conjecture: $C(K)$ is finite for any curve $C/K$ of genus $\ge 2$.
questions.q: Faltings' theorem (1983, *Endlichkeitssätze für abelsche Varietäten*) gives finiteness for which set, in any number field $K$ with $g\ge 1$ and finite $S$ fixed?
choices: All abelian varieties of dimension $g$ over $K$ — without restriction.
Isomorphism classes of $g$-dimensional principally polarized abelian varieties over $K$ with good reduction outside $S$.
Isogeny classes of $g$-dimensional abelian varieties with semistable reduction at every place.
Smooth projective varieties of dimension $g$ over $K$.

questions.explain: Faltings simultaneously proved Mordell, Tate's isogeny conjecture, and semisimplicity — all three are theorems of *Endlichkeitssätze*. BSD remains open: it is a different beast involving $L$-values and is not implied by Faltings.
questions.q: Which results are corollaries (or near-corollaries) of Faltings' 1983 paper? Select all that apply.
choices: Mordell's conjecture: $C(K)$ is finite for any smooth projective curve of genus $\ge 2$ over a number field.
Tate's isogeny conjecture for abelian varieties over number fields: $\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_\ell \to \mathrm{Hom}_{G_K}(T_\ell A, T_\ell B)$ is an isomorphism.
Semisimplicity of the Galois action on $T_\ell A \otimes \mathbb{Q}_\ell$ for $A/K$.
The full Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture.
